title: Workflow Platforms With Data Residency Controls: The Comparison Nobody Has Published
summary: Region pinning vs. air-gap: a 12-platform comparison of workflow automation data residency controls regulators actually audit.
body_markdown:
### Summary


- Data residency is a spectrum of deployment controls: region pinning is the weakest control, and air-gap is the only deployment mode that eliminates vendor-side processing risk entirely.
- Across 12 workflow platforms measured against 7 residency controls, most stop at region pinning; only UiPath, Camunda, n8n, and Jinba document support for disconnected, customer-controlled operation.
- Control-plane residency is the most overlooked gap: a platform can process production data in-region while routing orchestration, configuration, and audit logs through another jurisdiction.
- Ask about residency in the first vendor conversation: confirm where data lives at rest, in transit, and in the control plane, and whether vendor personnel can access execution data at all.
- For regulated enterprises that need air-gapped or on-premises deployment,[Jinba Flow](https://flow.jinba.io/) keeps execution, control plane, and AI inference inside your own perimeter, with SOC II compliance and human approval gates on every knowledge update.


Compliance teams in regulated operations are being caught off guard. A workflow automation project ships, the platform runs in the vendor's preferred region, and then the audit arrives. Every data flow crossing a jurisdictional boundary needs mapping. Legal sign-off is required on each one. In some cases, a client demands a local-only solution and the integration stack has to be rebuilt from scratch.


The root cause is almost always the same: data residency was treated as a detail to resolve later, not a selection criterion from the start.


The comparison that would prevent this does not exist in any single place. Buyers evaluating workflow automation data residency have to open twelve vendor trust centers, read twelve sets of documentation, and assemble the picture by hand. This article does that work once, side by side, for the platforms regulated buyers actually evaluate.


## Data Residency Is a Spectrum, Not a Checkbox


Before the table, the framework. "Data residency support" means different things at different points on a control spectrum, and the difference between those points determines whether your platform can satisfy a regulator.


The spectrum runs in one direction:


1. **Region pinning** : the vendor places your data in a data center within a named geography. The vendor controls the infrastructure. You select a region; the vendor manages everything beneath it.
2. **Private cloud / BYOC** : the platform runs in a cloud account you own, giving you more infrastructure visibility but still cloud-dependent.
3. **Self-hosted on customer infrastructure** : the platform runs on servers you operate. Execution data, credentials, and the workflow database live in infrastructure you control entirely.
4. **Air-gapped self-host** : the platform runs on your infrastructure with no outbound connection to vendor services, license servers, or the public internet.


Region pinning is the weakest form of data residency control. Air-gapped self-hosting is the strongest. Most vendor marketing collapses this spectrum into a single claim.


### What region pinning actually delivers


[Workato's EU data center announcement](https://www.workato.com/the-connector/eu-data-center/) is a clear example of what region pinning means in practice. Workato places customer data and core AI capabilities in its EU data center. The customer gets geographic placement. The customer does not get custody of execution. The vendor's infrastructure team retains full control of the environment, the runtime, and the update cycle.


This satisfies some regulations. It does not satisfy the requirement that no vendor personnel can access execution data, and it does not support an air-gap requirement.


### What self-hosting actually delivers


[n8n's self-hosting documentation](https://docs.n8n.io/hosting/) is organised around the concerns of an infrastructure owner: database configuration, environment variables, credential encryption, user management, and security hardening. That organisation is itself a signal. Execution data, credentials, and the workflow database live in infrastructure the customer controls, not in n8n's cloud. A buyer can inspect the database schema, rotate encryption keys, and manage users without contacting the vendor.


Self-hosting is not automatically equivalent to air-gap. A self-hosted instance may still call out to a vendor's license server, telemetry endpoint, or update service. Air-gap closes those connections. UiPath's Automation Suite documentation includes a[dedicated deployment architecture page](https://docs.uipath.com/automation-suite/automation-suite/2022.10/installation-guide/deployment-architecture) for offline installation, treating air-gap as a first-class deployment mode rather than an edge case.


### The control-plane blind spot


One axis the spectrum above does not capture on its own is control-plane residency. The control plane is where orchestration metadata, scheduling, audit logs, and configuration live. A platform can process your production data in-region while routing control-plane traffic through a different jurisdiction entirely.


[MuleSoft Anypoint](https://medium.com/slalom-australia/deployment-models-for-mulesoft-implementations-58a99f51937f) makes this explicit: the platform offers three deployment models (fully vendor-managed, fully customer-managed, and hybrid) precisely because the control plane and the runtime plane are separate architectural concerns. Most other vendors do not surface this distinction. Buyers need to ask for it directly.


## The Comparison: 12 Workflow Platforms, 7 Data Residency Controls


The columns below map directly to the spectrum above. Each column tests a distinct layer of control.


- **Region pinning:** Can buyers select the geographic region for their SaaS instance?
- **Data-at-rest residency:** Is stored customer data confirmed to remain within a specific jurisdiction?
- **In-transit residency:** Is data processing confirmed to remain in-jurisdiction while the data is in motion, including during workflow execution?
- **Control-plane residency:** Can the orchestration and management layer be run within the buyer's jurisdiction or infrastructure?
- **Self-host / on-prem:** Can the full platform run on infrastructure the buyer operates?
- **Air-gap support:** Is there a documented, supported path for running the platform with no outbound connection to vendor services?
- **Audit logging:** Are structured logs available that satisfy a compliance audit?

## What This Table Shows


The majority of platforms on this list stop at region pinning. Salesforce Hyperforce, Workato, ServiceNow, and the Microsoft Power Platform all let buyers select a region for their SaaS instance. For each of them, the control plane remains vendor-managed and the in-transit processing guarantee applies only within that vendor's environment, not within the buyer's infrastructure perimeter.


[Microsoft Power Platform data residency regions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/power-platform/admin/data-residency) address where data at rest is stored across its geography boundaries, and on-premises data gateways extend some connectivity inward. But the orchestration layer, the logic execution, and the AI features of Copilot Studio remain cloud-resident. The gateway is a connector, not a self-hosted runtime.


[Salesforce Hyperforce](https://www.salesforce.com/hyperforce/) is worth examining separately. Moving an org to Hyperforce changes IP ranges, affects integration allow-lists, and can break existing connector configurations. Teams that have gone through the migration report measurable administrative overhead and, in some cases, broken integrations that require remediation. Hyperforce delivers region pinning and encryption at rest, but the control plane and runtime remain on Salesforce infrastructure.


MuleSoft Anypoint shifts the picture for control-plane residency. Because the Anypoint platform separates its control plane from its runtime plane by design, buyers who need the orchestration layer inside their own boundary can achieve it by running the runtime in customer-managed infrastructure while selecting a hybrid or fully customer-managed model. This is the most architecturally honest approach to control-plane residency in the SaaS segment.


Boomi offers a self-managed runtime through its[Molecule installer](https://boomi.com/platform/molecule/) , which runs within a customer's private cloud or on-premises environment. The Boomi control plane remains vendor-managed. The runtime plane can be customer-controlled. That is a meaningful distinction from purely cloud-native platforms, though it falls short of a fully self-managed control plane.


True self-hosting with a customer-managed control plane narrows the list to UiPath Automation Suite, Camunda self-managed, and n8n. Among those, documented air-gap support further narrows it: UiPath includes an offline installation path in its Automation Suite deployment architecture documentation;[Camunda self-managed](https://docs.camunda.io/docs/self-managed/about-self-managed/) is designed for environments where network egress is restricted; n8n's self-hosted model, by design, keeps all execution within the customer's infrastructure.


Air-gap is the rarest capability on this list. It is also the only deployment mode that eliminates the residency risk entirely. A region-pinned instance can have its data processed by vendor engineers. An air-gapped instance cannot.


## For Regulated Buyers Who Cannot Compromise: Jinba


Jinba is SOC II compliant and built with on-premises and air-gapped deployment as core capabilities, not configuration options added after the fact. For financial institutions and insurance operators where internal data cannot leave the security perimeter, this architectural commitment is the starting point, not a premium tier.


**Deployment and infrastructure control**


Jinba supports full on-premises deployment, air-gapped deployment, RBAC, SSO, and audit logging. Private AI model hosting is available through AWS Bedrock, Azure AI, and fully self-hosted options, which means the AI inference layer also remains within the buyer's infrastructure perimeter. No component of the Jinba stack is required to call out to a vendor-managed cloud service.


**Knowledge integrity and auditability**


Jinba Brain is Jinba's knowledge layer. It is not a retrieval-augmented generation system and does not use vector embeddings. It stores company knowledge as ontology-validated, linked records, using FIBO (EDM Council Financial Industry Business Ontology) for banking and the ACORD Information Model for insurance as base-layer schemas.


Raw source data is kept unmodified and on-premises. The pipeline reads it; it never alters or relocates it. Every record carries its source path and a SHA-256 hash, giving auditors a complete chain of traceability back to the originating document.


No update to the knowledge base is applied automatically. Every proposed revision requires a human approval gate before it goes live, and the full history of every change is retained. This is the hard governance requirement that distinguishes a validated knowledge layer from a general-purpose data search tool.


**Workflow automation data residency at the execution layer**


Jinba Flow publishes workflows as APIs, batch processes, or MCP servers. Jinba's deterministic execution model runs approximately 80% of workflow steps as rule-based processes. At scale, this runs at $5 to $20 per month, compared to $300 or more for equivalent stochastic AI agent execution. The 15 to 60 times cost difference is a consequence of architecture, not optimisation: deterministic execution does not require repeated LLM inference for steps that have known, validated outputs.


Jinba App Neo adds governed, shared Claude agents for a team, built on Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5.5. Approval steps (designated as WAIT_FOR_APPROVAL in the execution model) pause a run until a human approves or rejects via an in-chat approval card or the run console. Credentials are never passed to the AI layer.


## Choosing the Right Point on the Spectrum


Workflow automation data residency is decided by the weakest link in the platform's architecture, not the strongest claim in its marketing. Region pinning satisfies geographic placement requirements. It does not satisfy requirements for infrastructure custody, control-plane residency, or disconnected operation.


The selection criteria for platforms with workflow automation data residency controls should follow the actual compliance requirement:


- If the regulation requires data to remain in a named jurisdiction: verify that both data-at-rest storage and in-transit processing are confirmed for that jurisdiction, including for the control plane.
- If the regulation requires that vendor personnel cannot access execution data: self-hosted deployment on customer infrastructure is the minimum viable option.
- If the regulation or security policy requires no external connectivity: documented air-gap support is the requirement, not a preference.


For most regulated enterprises, the decision reduces to a practical shortlist. Platforms that offer only region pinning cannot meet the second or third requirement. Platforms with self-hosting but no air-gap support cannot meet the third. Among the twelve platforms compared here, only Camunda self-managed, UiPath Automation Suite, n8n, and Jinba provide documented support for disconnected, customer-controlled operation.


Among those, only Jinba combines air-gapped and on-premises deployment with SOC II compliance, private AI model hosting, an ontology-validated knowledge layer with SHA-256 hash traceability, and hard human approval gates at every knowledge update, the combination that regulated financial and insurance operations specifically require.


Ask about data residency in the first vendor conversation, not after the architecture is in production. The audit process is significantly more expensive than the selection process.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is data residency in workflow automation?


Data residency in workflow automation is the practice of keeping execution data, credentials, workflow metadata, and control-plane information within a specific jurisdiction or infrastructure boundary. It goes beyond where data is stored at rest and includes where workflows are processed, where orchestration and audit logs live, and whether vendor personnel or vendor-managed services can access execution data. In regulated environments, data residency is a compliance requirement, not an infrastructure preference.


### Why does data residency matter for regulated industries?


Data residency matters because regulators and internal security policies often require sensitive data to remain within a named jurisdiction or inside a controlled infrastructure perimeter. Financial institutions and insurance operators may also need to demonstrate that vendor personnel cannot access execution data and that the platform can operate without external connectivity. A workflow automation platform that cannot meet those requirements creates audit exposure, remediation costs, and in some cases forces a rebuild of the integration stack.


### What is the difference between region pinning and self-hosting for data residency?


Region pinning places customer data in a vendor-managed data center within a selected geography, while self-hosting runs the platform on infrastructure the customer operates. Region pinning gives geographic placement but leaves the vendor in control of the runtime, infrastructure, and update cycle. Self-hosting gives the customer custody of execution data, credentials, and the workflow database, but it is not automatically air-gapped unless outbound connections to vendor services are also removed.


### What is control-plane residency and why does it matter?


Control-plane residency is the location and control of the orchestration layer where scheduling, configuration, audit logs, and workflow metadata live. It matters because a platform can process production data in-region while routing control-plane traffic through a different jurisdiction. Regulated buyers should ask whether the control plane can run within their jurisdiction or infrastructure, not just whether the runtime can be region-pinned.


### Can a region-pinned SaaS platform satisfy data residency compliance?


A region-pinned SaaS platform can satisfy some geographic placement requirements, but it cannot satisfy every data residency obligation. Region pinning may confirm where data is stored at rest, but the vendor typically retains control of the runtime, control plane, and update cycle. It does not by itself prove that vendor personnel cannot access execution data, and it does not support air-gap requirements where no external connectivity is allowed.


### Which workflow automation platforms support self-hosting and air-gap deployment?


Among the platforms compared in this article, UiPath Automation Suite, Camunda self-managed, n8n, and Jinba provide documented support for customer-controlled or disconnected operation. For full self-hosting with a customer-managed control plane, the article narrows the list to UiPath, Camunda, and n8n. Documented air-gap support is available from UiPath, Camunda, n8n, and Jinba, making air-gap the rarest and strongest data residency control in the comparison.


### What is air-gap support and when is it required?


Air-gap support is a documented deployment mode in which the platform runs with no outbound connection to vendor services, license servers, telemetry endpoints, or the public internet. It is required when a regulation or security policy prohibits external connectivity from the environment that processes sensitive data. Air-gap is the only deployment mode that eliminates the risk of vendor-side data processing entirely, because an air-gapped instance cannot call out to a vendor-managed service.


### How does Jinba support workflow automation data residency?


Jinba supports workflow automation data residency through on-premises and air-gapped deployment, with execution, control plane, and AI inference kept inside the buyer's perimeter. Jinba is SOC II compliant and includes RBAC, SSO, audit logging, and private AI model hosting through AWS Bedrock, Azure AI, or fully self-hosted options. Its knowledge layer, Jinba Brain, stores ontology-validated records with SHA-256 hash traceability and human approval gates, while Jinba Flow runs deterministic workflows without requiring vendor-managed cloud services.


### What should regulated buyers ask vendors about data residency before selection?


Regulated buyers should ask where data is stored at rest, where data is processed in transit, where the control plane runs, whether the platform can be self-hosted, whether air-gap deployment is documented, and whether audit logs satisfy compliance review. They should also ask whether vendor personnel can access execution data and whether AI inference or knowledge processing calls out to a vendor-managed service. Asking these questions during vendor selection is significantly cheaper than discovering the gaps during an audit.
